newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Canadian woman appeals death sentence in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Canadian woman appeals death sentence in Vietnam.

text.p: A Canadian national has appealed against the death sentence that a Hanoi court handed down earlier this month after finding her guilty of trafficking in heroin, a Canadian diplomat said on Monday.
The woman's Vietnamese mother, who was sentenced to life in prison for the same crime, has also appealed.

Nguyen Thi Hiep of Montreal and Tran Thi Cam were arrested last April at Hanoi airport as they checked in for a flight to Hong Kong. They were charged with attempting to take 5.45 kg (12 lb) of heroin out of the country.
Under Vietnamese law, trafficking in as little as one kg (2.2 lb) of heroin is punishable by death, normally in front of a firing squad.
In addition to their death and life imprisonment sentences, the 41-year-old Canadian woman was fined one billion dong ($86,000) and her 71-year-old mother was fined 500 million dong.
Hiep, who was reported by local newspapers to have left Vietnam in 1982 and gained Canadian nationality in 1985, is still considered by Hanoi as a Vietnamese citizen.
The diplomat said Canadian officials were allowed to visit her last July but had not been granted consular access since then.
Separately, two Hong Kong citizens were sentenced to death by a court in Ho Chi Minh City last Friday for drug-trafficking.
Both holders of British passports, the two were arrested at Ho Chi Minh City airport in March 1996 after 18.1 kg (40 pounds) of heroin was found concealed in false-bottomed cases.
Sun Chi Kin and Chan Chun Hung Sammy, like the Canandian woman and her mother, were given 15 days to appeal.
The first foreigner to be sentenced to death for drug trafficking in Vietnam was a Hong Kong man in 1995.

Drugs experts say Vietnam is both a growing market and a transit route for narcotics from the Golden Triangle opium-poppy growing area, which straddles the borders of Laos, Burma and Thailand. Heroin is derived from opium.
